author_list: Kozlov, MV; Filippov, BY; Zubrij, NA; Zverev, V
title: Abrupt changes in invertebrate herbivory on woody plants at the forest-tundra ecotone
habitat_type_comments: several sites: Vaygach Island - graminoid prostrate dwarf-shrub tundra; Belyi Nos Peninsula - low shrub tundra; Kolguev Island - low shrub tundra; Murmansk - forest-tundra ecotone; Naryan-Mar - forest-tundra ecotone
herbivore_data_comments: presence/absence of different feeding guilds of invertebrate herbivores assessed based on damage types
comment: COORDINATES: observational study using several tundra and forest-tundra sites, each qith different "herbivore diversity". Site coordinates reported here are the centroid (eyeballed from map). Original coordinates are reported in Table 1 (sites Vaygach Island, Belyi Nos Peninsula, Kolguev Island, Murmansk, Naryan-Mar). ELEVATION is calculated as the average of the five sites. SPATIAL_EXTENT roughly calculated from map, from the polygon encompassing the five sites (~1000 km x 200 km rectangle). SPATIAL_RESOLUTION up to 1x1 m because data are reported at plant individual level
more_data: measures of foliar damage are reported as well as the proportion of leaves damaged by insects (DL); only values for LA are reported here
measured_response_comments: percentage of leaf area damaged or removed by invertebrate herbivores (reported in study as LA)
bias_risk_comments: CRITERION 1: medium risk because of study design using different sites with different habitats and overall conditions that can affect the composition of herbivore assemblages and the intensity of herbivory (outcome) but the main potential confounding variables (habitat, average temperature, precipitation) are reported in the study. CRITERION 5 medium risk because it is unclear if researcher was aware of research question.

author_list: Den Herder, M; Virtanen, R; Roininen, H
title: Effects of reindeer browsing on tundra willow and its associated insect herbivores
habitat_type_comments: habitat not clearly described but mentions thickets of willow scrubs
herbivore_data_comments: mention abundance data from other sources
contrast: invertebrate_herbivores; large_herbivores; medium_herbivores; small_herbivores | invertebrate_herbivores; medium_herbivores; small_herbivores
contrast_f: F2; F3; inv | F2; F3; inv
comment: here I extract values for “Old, fenced” (black triangles; this is our “lower_diversity” level) and “Old, open to reindeer” (open triangles; this is our “higher_diversity” level); we are not interested in the “Rejuvenated” plants because they received additional manipulations. Finally, we are only interested in year 2002 (last measurement).
bias_risk_comments: CRITERION 2 medium risk because it is unclear how they selected the sites and blocks within the sites. Within blocks they selected their willow ramets randomly. CRITERION 5 medium risk because it is unclear if researcher was aware of research question. CRITERION 7 medium risk because it is unclear if researcher was aware of levels of herbivore diversity in the different treatments.

title: Two arctic tundra graminoids differ in tolerance to herbivory when grown with added soil nutrients
study_design_comments: the experiment also included NP additions (not reported here)
herbivore_data_comments: authors report presence of herbivores and some qualitative assessment
comment: the experimental set up at Toolik Lake has size selective exclosures but here they only use the small fences (excluding all herbivores). ADDITIONAL EXPOSURES - fertilizer addition (NP). In the paper they also report data for Hierochloe alpina in the DH habitat, but results are only for NP plots, so we cannot include here. Only data for MAT habitat are extracted.
more_data: there is also data from 2004 and 2005
bias_risk_comments: CRITERION 7 unclear whether data analyst was unaware of treatments

study_design_comments: the experiment also included NP additions (not reported here)
herbivore_data_comments: mammalian activity was estimated in all plots

author_list: Kitti, H; Forbes, BC; Oksanen, J
title: Long- and short-term effects of reindeer grazing on tundra wetland vegetation
soil_moisture_comments: Described as 'water-saturated virtually throughout the growing season'
study_design_comments: Experimental: 4-year exclosures within the year-round pastures in Finland. Control and exclusion plots were randomly assigned to treatments. The study was conducted along the fence.
herbivore_data_comments: They report 10-12 reindeer km2, but without a source. This would be the contrast between year-round pasture and short-term exclosures built within those
outcome_comments: I think this contrast should be interpreted as short-term effects (4 years) of the removal of reindeer on vegetation. Notice that reindeer exclosures were in place year-round and located in Finland (year-round pastures), thus this contrast should refer to 4 years of both summer and winter exclusion of reindeer
bias_risk_comments: C3-4: medium risk because the study was conducted along a fence. It is now well established that reindeer use these areas more than an area selected randomly within the same pasture. In other words, areas along fences often overestimate the grazing pressure at the study site, and thus are not representative of the actual grazing pressure; C7: they have a two-hierarchical, nested design, with the following structure: site/Trt_ID(plot), as measurements are taken in 4 subplots (sampling unit) within plots. However, it seems to me they only include one level of the hierarchy in the random factor, i.e. Trt_ID(plot), and they do not nest this latter within Site.

title: Long-Term Experiments Reveal Strong Interactions Between Lemmings and Plants in the Fennoscandian Highland Tundra
herbivore_data_comments: rodent populations were surveyed by snap-trapping
more_data: the figures also present proportions of different plant functional groups, but no errors associated to the measurements; in the text there are statistical analyses for the cover and biomass of functional groups, but the models include interactions, so cannot really extract data from them...
measured_response_comments: in Figure 2 y-axis shows "cover value" but it is nr of hits/100; for groups other than mosses and lichens they recorded multiple hits/pin, so this is a measure of abundance. Sampling area is 20 x 20 cm, 100 pins
bias_risk_comments: CRITERION 1: not mention how the study sites were selected, but within the area plots were selected subjectvely to represent variability in vegetation, so potentially capturing the effects of other potentially confounding variables. CRITERION 5: unclear whether awareness of the study question could influence measurements. CRITERION 7: unclear whether the data analyst was aware of the levels of diversity applied

soil_moisture_comments: Are usually water-saturated early in the growing season, but with lower water as the season progresses

author_list: Metcalfe, DB; Olofsson, J
title: Distinct impacts of different mammalian herbivore assemblages on arctic tundra CO2 exchange during the peak of the growing season
locality: Study site is 5km from Abisko in northern Sweden. Dwarf shrub heath tundra.
soil_moisture_comments: Soil moisture is directly measured and compared for different herbivore exposures. Reported as 44.5% (grazed control); 32% (large herbivores excluded); 50.3% (large and small herbivores excluded).
comment: The study also assessed the effects of soil temperature, vegetation and total biomass on GPP, R (respiration) and NEE (net ecosystem exchange of CO2).  It uses data on small herbivore densities from a prior study (Olofsson et al 2013) and reindeer density from Olofsson et al. 2004.
outcome_comments: ICB: Data extracted from Figure 1; there are also values presened in Table 1 (extracted by JR) but they are different -- I extract from Fig.1 to be comparable to NEE and R
statistical_test: linear mixed effects model with a block factor
effect_size_direction: low vs high diversity (typical in exclosure studies)
bias_risk_comments: Criterion 1: Samples taken in a year when the microtine rodent population was particularly low (but see comment).  Criterion 6: Medium due to unreported subgroups of data. The authors report that soil mineral N and P levels were measured, but unreported. It's unclear why this data is not reported: "we find no significant difference among treatments in other potentially limiting factors such as soil temperature and moisture (Table 1), or soil mineral N and P (Metcalfe and Olofsson unpubl.)".         Criterion 7: comes out as medium risk due to use of inferential statistics and analyst aware of herbivore diversity levels in the different units.

soil_moisture_comments: Soil moisture is directly measured and compared for different herbivore exposures. Reported as 44.5% (grazed control); 32% (large herbivores excluded); 50.3% (large and small herbivores excluded).
bias_risk_comments: Criterion 1: Samples taken in a year when the microtine rodent population was particularly low (but see comment).  Criterion 6: Medium due to unreported subgroups of data. The authors report that soil mineral N and P levels were measured, but unreported. It's unclear why this data is not reported: "we find no significant difference among treatments in other potentially limiting factors such as soil temperature and moisture (Table 1), or soil mineral N and P (Metcalfe and Olofsson unpubl.)".         Criterion 7: comes out as medium risk due to use of inferential statistics and analyst aware of herbivore diversity levels in the different units.

author_list: Lara, MJ; Johnson, DR; Andresen, C; Hollister, RD; Tweedie, CE
title: Peak season carbon exchange shifts from a sink to a source following 50+years of herbivore exclusion in an Arctic tundra ecosystem
locality: Northernmost point of the Alaskan Arctic Coastal Plain near the town of Barrow
habitat_type_comments: Includes 'seasonally flooded graminoid tundra' and 'wet graminoid tundra'
study_design_comments: They are using exclosures established in the late 1950s (>50 years), and no details are provided on whether the two treatment levels (C and E) were assigned to plots randomly. Yet, there's other literature that used this experiment, and hence one might want to check whether the study design is better explained somewhere else.
comment: Additional comments: (1) data were collected 2 years after a lemming population high; (2) I think, in general, the heterogeneity of variances have not been taken into consideration properly (have a look at SSD, where it was 0 for dry habitat (+-0 SE), yet it was included in the analysis); (3) You might want to check papers from Lara (2012 and 2014) to see whether some data are duplicated (it is not mentioned in the paper, though)
more_data: They report the effects of herbivore exclusion on soil temperature (and the ANOVA table is presented), but then these data are not visualized and it is not possible to extract actual values. No further action to be taken.
outcome_comments: Notice that they used ANOVA because the model included the two-way interaction between HERBIVORY and HABITAT. Thus, I'm reporting here the F value for HERBIVORY, but notice that it is little representative because the interaction between the two factors could be significant (i.e./e.g. the herbivory F-value might be high enough for a significant difference, but for a particular habitat the difference was not detected). Conversely, I'm reporting the p-values they give for each HERBIVORY contrast within habitat, and thus these might be more valuable here
measured_response_comments: Depth of thaw using protocols from the Circumpolar Active Layer Monitoring Program (negative values)
bias_risk_comments: C2: medium risk because it is unclear whether plots were randomly assigned to treatment levels; C7: medium risk because plots are grouped in two distinct sites, which however are analyzed together without accounting for the spatial dependency they introduce + plots belonging to the prostrate-shrub tundra are found in one site only (but they are used as if they were in both)

more_data: Table with linear models for more parameters of the soil, but comparing the 3 herbivories, so it is not useful
bias_risk_comments: They only check the herbivory of moth larvae (but they do not take into account other herbivores? Not clear, but there is not exclosures).

author_list: Ylanne, H; Kaarlejarvi, E; Vaisanen, M; Mannisto, MK; Ahonen, SHK; Olofsson, J; Stark, S
title: Removal of grazers alters the response of tundra soil carbon to warming and enhanced nitrogen availability
soil_texture_comments: Authors say 'This in a non-permafrost area with glacial tills as the dominant mineral soil type. As typical for tundra soils, only weak podzolic profiles are developed - organic layer of approx. 4.25 cm (Ylanne et al., 2018)'
soil_moisture_comments: Further details might be found in te Beest et al., 2016
soil_type: Shallow podzolic profile developed above mineral soil
habitat_type_comments: Described as a mixture from exposed ridges to moist snow beds
study_design_comments:
Experimental: In 2010, we set up eight blocks bisecting the fence. The blocks were 5 m x 10 m, spaced 20 m apart. To each block, we set four plots (approx. 1 m2) on both sides of the fence (HG and LG) with the randomly assigned treatments of control (Ctrl), warming (W), fertilization (F), and  WF. Additionally, plots under HG were divided into grazed (HG) and ungrazed (HGexc) subplots with short-term exclosures (height 0.9 m, mesh 40 x 40 mm) that were built each year (2010–2014) before reindeer migration and removed after the grazing event.
Here, I report the contrast between excluded plots and grazed plots in HG
herbivore_data_comments: Further details might be found in the several papers cited in the 'study area' section, but it remains unclear whether a particular paper is cited for reindeer abundances. No information is provided on other herbivores besides reindeer.
more_data: They state they measured organic matter content and bulk density, but I didn't find these results reported in the Results section. Moreover, they report a few ANOVA results in the Appendix and main text about e.g. forb abundance, grass and sedge abundances separately, lichen, and for C stocks but neither raw values/summary statistics nor estimates are presented. No further action has been taken.
outcome_comments:
Statistical test reported is ANOVA (F value) from a multilevel model for mixed designs. Notice that the ANOVA also included the other levels of herbivory (LG) tested for a given response variable, and thus the P-value to be used is the one in parentheses, which refers to the post-hoc comparison of interest.

Authors probably forgot to report here what contrast the P-value (hence significance) refers to.
measured_response_comments: Number of total hits (normalized on 100 pins); 80, 40  or 20 pins per plot (depending on treatment), multiple hits per pin --> abundance
bias_risk_comments: C6: Medium risk because of two reasons: (1) Authors failed a few times in reporting all the contrasts of interest (and related effect sizes, mean differences, etc) in Tables (e.g. when three sampling occasions were included in the analyses), and thus it was sometimes complicated to understand whether the extraced contrast was meaningful or not; (2) Authors always reported ANOVA tables with all the effects (including interaction effects that were not significant). While I might see the reason, that complicates a lot the interpretation of the main effects (and can of course change substantially the results obtained)

author_list: Hjalten, J; Roininen, H; Danell, K; Price, PW
title: Distribution and oviposition preference of galling sawflies in arctic Canada
habitat_type_comments: Arctic shrub tundra zone (dominated by Carex, Dryas and Eriophorum)
diversity_contrast_comments: they looked at shoots within the same ramet with and without galls
comment: I was hesitating a bit with this study -- they report the response variable (shoot length, nr of leaves) but interpret them the other way around, i.e. insects show preference for ovipositing on longer shoots
measured_response_variable: shoot length Salix reticulata per ramet
bias_risk_comments: CRITERION 1: there might be confounding variables but these are associated to the study being observational ; by sampling the same ramet the effect of these confounding variables is likely to be minimal. CRITERION 2: medium risk because it is unclear how they selected individual plants. CRITERION 3: herbivore diversity levels were defined based on the presence (or absence) of particular galls. CRITERION 5: unclear whether the measured response would capture the effects of herbivores (actually the authors interpret it the other way around, i.e. insects show preference for ovipositing on longer shoots). CRITERION 7 unclear whether data analyst was unaware of treatments.

author_list: Rinnan, R; Stark, S; Tolvanen, A
title: Responses of vegetation and soil microbial communities to warming and simulated herbivory in a subarctic heath
habitat_type_comments:
The
field layer vegetation of the experimental site is dominated by the
deciduous dwarf shrub V. myrtillus (approximately 40% cover) and
evergreen dwarf shrubs Empetrum nigrum L. (15%) and V. vitis-idaea
L. (5%). Understorey vegetation is dominated by Dicranum spp.
mosses (20%), and Cladina spp. (10%) and Stereocaulon spp. (5%)
lichens.
diversity_contrast_comments: Wounding of the dominant deciduous dwarf shrub Vaccinium myrtillus L. to simulate insect herbivory
herbivore_data_comments:
We measured vegetation
cover in 2003 and 2007, soil nutrient concentrations in 2003 and 2006, soil microbial respiration in
2003, and composition and function of soil microbial communities in 2006.
bias_risk_comments: It is unclear whether further herbivory apart from the simulation might have taken place in the plots.

author_list: Van der Wal, R; Brooker, RW
title: Mosses mediate grazer impacts on grass abundance in arctic ecosystems
locality: 14 locations across Spitspbergen. Reporting here the location of  Skansbukta as it's in the centre of all recorded locations.
soil_moisture_comments:
from very dry (10%) to water-saturated
(60%) soils
habitat_type_comments:
A central
transect was set out from the bottom of each valley, up
the valley sides, until plant cover became very patchy. No particular habitat type is provided in the text.
study_design_comments:
Sites were selected on the
basis of available information on Reindeer numbers in
the archipelago, with the aim of surveying areas with
widely differing Reindeer densities.
herbivore_data_comments:
We used pellet group density as a measure of Reindeer occurrence. All Reindeer
pellet groups within a 2 m wide band along the full length
of the transect were counted. Data were expressed as
number of pellet groups per km transect length.
comment: This study includes 3 methods: reindeer exclusion in a single area, observations over 14 areas with varying densities of reindeer, and a glasshouse experiment. This column reports on rthe 14 areas with varying densities of reindeer. Total cover of vascular plants was unrelated to Reindeer density across 14 sites throughout Spitsbergen, but the model refers to different values of reindeer density so not including those estimates here.
outcome_comments: Values extracted from Fig 4. Values for the low diversity field are the mean of the two points where reindeer density index = 0, and the value for high diversity is the maximum value of reindeer density. Abundance of grasses was positively related to Reindeer density: where Reindeer were absent or scarce, average grass cover was low; but with greater index of Reindeer presence at a site, grasses were significantly more abundant (non-linear regression: F = 18·47, df = 1,10, P < 0·005). Not including these model results as they include different densities of reindeer grazing.
measured_response_comments: Abundance of grasses (corrected for total plant cover) at sites with contrasting reindeer densities (estimated as faecal pellet group density)
bias_risk_comments: Some other herbivores are mentioned in the Introduction, but it is not clear if any other herbivores have contributed to the overall herbivory of the places with varying densities of reindeer grazing.

author_list: Olofsson, J; Hulme, PE; Oksanen, L; Suominen, O
title: Effects of mammalian herbivores on revegetation of disturbed areas in the forest-tundra ecotone in northern Fennoscandia
country_comments: 2 sites in Norway, 2 sites in Sweden (coordinates in final comments)
habitat_type_comments: forest and tundra plots pooled together
herbivore_data_comments: Microtine rodent densities were studied by snap-trapping in spring and autumn and the abundance of all other vertebrate herbivores was estimated by collecting faeces (see Olofsson et al. 2004b for more details).
comment: Locations of the study (3 plots per location, being control, large mesh and small mesh): Abisko lat. 68.3230556, long. 18.865833333333335, 550-600 (m.a.s.l.); Vassijávri lat. 68.4405556, long. 18.27472222222222, 460-500 (m.a.s.l.); Joatka lat. 69.7530556, long. 24, 450 (m.a.s.l.); Seiland  lat. 70.5061111, long. 23.528055555555554, 100 (ms.a.s.l.). Voles and lemmings were found on some occasions in Abisko and Vássijávri: the effect of the small mesh size exclosures might, therefore, be underestimated in these locations. Characteristics of the study areas are reported neither in this article, nor in Olofsson 2004a. Studies report recovery after disturbance!
measured_response_comments: abundance of plants was measured with point intercept but is expressed as % cover
bias_risk_comments: Some voles have entered in the small mammals exclosure at two sites (see comments below)

author_list: Cooper, EJ
title: Reindeer grazing reduces seed and propagule bank in the High Arctic
journal: CANADIAN JOURNAL OF BOTANY-REVUE CANADIENNE DE BOTANIQUE
elevation: All sampling sites were under 50 m asl (but not specified)
habitat_type_comments:
Three habitats:
(i) a ridge underneath a north-facing bird cliff dominated by lichen and Salix polaris, (ii) an exposed ridge dominated by Dryas octopetala and Silene acaulis, and
(iii) a moderate snowbed dominated by Salix polaris and Saxifraga oppositifolia
study_design_comments:
Reindeer exclosures (10 m x 10 m, 2 m high) were established prior to
the release of reindeer on Brøggerhalvøya in 1978
herbivore_data_comments:
In 1978, 15
Svalbard reindeer were introduced into Brøggerhalvøya (Øritsland and Alendal 1986). The population increased rapidly,
reaching a maximum of 360 animals in 1993 (Aanes et al.
2002). Sarsøyra, an adjacent lightly grazed peninsula with a similar climate, was colonized by about 40 reindeer from Brøggerhalvøya in the winter of 1993. The reindeer arrived either
over sea ice or by following the snowmobile tracks on the
glaciers. This population increased to 100 animals by spring
1999 (Henriksen et al. 2003).
comment: In text: latitude: 78.7166667 - 78.95; longitude: 11.3333333333333 - 12.333333333333334; here we used the centroid
outcome_comments: There were more germinating species per sample inside the fences than outside, this approached significance. Values from page 1743
reported_units: nr of germinating species per sample
measured_response_variable: Germinating species per sample - all habitats

author_list: Speed, JDM; Cooper, EJ; Jonsdottir, IS; van der Wal, R; Woodin, SJ
title: Plant community properties predict vegetation resilience to herbivore disturbance in the Arctic
soil_moisture_comments: Six of these communities were ona gradient of soil moisture, the seventh was a salt marsh; moss cover,moss depth (including live and senescing parts of moss shoots) andsoil moisture (conductivity measured with a Delta T theta probe) inthese seven communities are summarized in Table 1
study_design_comments: Three levels of disturbance intensity treatments were applied (Low, mid, high) and undisturbed controls selected. Low-intensity grubbing disturbance was implementedusing a sharpened 20 mm diameter steel tube inserted to a depth of50 mm and twisted to remove and export contents from the plot;this treatment was applied in a regular fashion to 31% of the plotarea. In the mid-intensity treatment 50% of the vegetation wasremoved by knife with the remainder being fragmented across theplot using the steel tube. High-intensity disturbance was created byusing a knife to remove 100% of the vegetation to a depth of50 mm.
herbivore_data_comments: grubbing by geese in Svalbard described based on another reference
more_data: There is also data on recovery of vegetation after three years (Figure 4)
outcome_comments: Figure 1; high intensity (high diversity) vs control (low diversity)
bias_risk_comments: NA

soil_moisture_comments: Six of these communities were ona gradient of soil moisture, the seventh was a salt marsh; moss cover,moss depth (including live and senescing parts of moss shoots) andsoil moisture (conductivity measured with a Delta T theta probe) inthese seven communities are summarized in Table 8
study_design_comments: Three levels of disturbance intensity treatments were applied (Low, mid, high) and undisturbed controls selected. Low-intensity grubbing disturbance was implementedusing a sharpened 20 mm diameter steel tube inserted to a depth of50 mm and twisted to remove and export contents from the plot;this treatment was applied in a regular fashion to 31% of the plotarea. In the mid-intensity treatment 50% of the vegetation wasremoved by knife with the remainder being fragmented across theplot using the steel tube. High-intensity disturbance was created byusing a knife to remove 100% of the vegetation to a depth of50 mm.
herbivore_data_comments: grubbing by geese in Svalbard described based on another reference
more_data: There is also data on recovery of vegetation after three years (Figure 4)
outcome_comments: Figure 1; high intensity (high diversity) vs control (low diversity)
bias_risk_comments: NA

locality: Adalvík, Grunnavík Nesdalur, Ingjaldssandur, Skálavík and Thorgeirsfjördur valleys

comment: "Within each zone, we covered the major topographical contrasts: landform curvature (small grain size),elevation (intermediate grain size) and slope aspect (large grain size).Alphasmall,alphaintermediate andalphalarge represent within community diversity on a small,intermediate and large spatial grain size. bias_risk_comments: NA

comment: The study also assesses the diet of muskoxen and the interaction between predator and prey (data not extractable).
outcome_comments: Spider numbers are extracted from Table 1. The number of spiders caught was similar among treatments (p = 0.68 and p = 0.57 for all spiders and spiders containing prey, respectively).
bias_risk_comments: It is unclear whether the fences exclude all mammals present in the area or not, thus there is the potential for some unaccounted grazing in the exclosure plots by small mammals. Additionally, the aim of the study is to evaluate the effect of herbivory on spider populations via vegetation change, but no vegetation results are provided.
quantitative_synthesis: not possible to estimate effect size

diversity_contrast_comments: "permanent muskox exclosures with five replicate blocks, each including an un-manipulated control and a fenced exclosure plot." It is not reported whether the fences are size-exclusive or not, so I assume no herbivores can penetrate the fence.
comment: The study also assesses the diet of muskoxen and the interaction between predator and prey (data not extractable).
outcome_comments: Spider numbers are extracted from Table 1. The number of spiders caught was similar among treatments (p = 0.68 and p = 0.57 for all spiders and spiders containing prey, respectively).
bias_risk_comments: It is unclear whether the fences exclude all mammals present in the area or not, thus there is the potential for some unaccounted grazing in the exclosure plots by small mammals. Additionally, the aim of the study is to evaluate the effect of herbivory on spider populations via vegetation change, but no vegetation results are provided.
quantitative_synthesis: not possible to estimate effect size

title: Reindeer grazing controls willows but has only minor effects on plant communities in Fennoscandian oroarctic mires
country_comments:
The experiment was carried out at ten study sites
near the border of Finland and Norway (68°49ʹ N, 23°49ʹ
E). Those coordinates show a point in Norway but there are plots both in Finland and in Norway for this study.
soil_texture_comments: There is mention of peat-accumulating fens
habitat_type_comments:
The mention to permafrost is that it's a "non-permafrost region", so not sure how to code that in the drop-down menu above. As for the habitat, "The landscape is a mosaic of
Betula nana–Cladina-type heaths and fjells and peat-accumulating
fens". So this could be coded as wetland or as prostrate shrub tundra.
study_design_comments: This study is an experimental approach comparing enclosures with open plots in the Finnish side, and then comparing with Norwegian plots where a fence along the Norway-Finland border stops reindeer from grazing during the summer. Reindeer are present in Norway during the winter but they mostly feed on dry habitats and thus grazing is considered to be virtually non-existent all year round.
diversity_contrast_comments: Both a fence between the Norwegian-Finnish border and then exclosures in the Finnish side. Only the comparison between enclosures and open plots in the Finnish side is reported here. --> study design is experimental and diversity contrast is exclosure
comment: Table 1 only shows an F-statistic and a p-value, and it's not specified if the significant difference in treatements is between grazed and exclosure or between grazed and nongrazed.
more_data: See note in row above, not sure if this qualifies as yes/no.
outcome_comments: Table 1 only shows an F-statistic and a p-value, and it's not specified if the significant difference in treatements is between grazed and exclosure or between grazed and nongrazed, so model results are not included. Means and variability are extracted from Figure 3. Value type of mean/median values and variability type are not specified, so a range of variability has been reported instead. --> ICB: since they are showing boxplots, the value should be median and the variability is the interquartile range (bottom of top to box)
reported_units: Number of pin hits in point-intercept method
measured_response_comments: one hit per pin (100 pins, 0.25 m2 plot) --> measure of cover
bias_risk_comments: It is specified that the non-grazed area in the Norwegian side might have experienced some unaccounted grazing during the summer. Grazing does take place on this area during the winter.

title: Mammalian herbivory shapes intraspecific trait responses to warmer climate and nutrient enrichment
habitat_type_comments: "The study site is characterized as species-rich tundra meadow dominated by grasses and forbs"
diversity_contrast_comments: "We implemented the herbivore exclusion treatment by establishing circular fences (160 cm in diameter, 100 cm in height, mesh size 10 × 10 mm) embedded 15 cm deep into the soil around each fenced plot (Kaarlejärvi et al., 2013). Additionally, we fenced the entire experimental area with a temporary reindeer fence from the beginning of August to the end of June in the following year. This was done to protect the experiment from straying reindeer outside the normal grazing season, and ensured that grazing pressure was similar in all plots (Kaarlejärvi et al., 2013)". It is not reported whether the fences are size-exclusive or not, so I assume no herbivores can penetrate the fence.
herbivore_data_comments: recent observations report 9-17 reindeer per km2
comment: This study assessed the effects of fertilization, warming and herbivory. Only ambient non-fertilized plots with and without grazing are reported here.
outcome_comments: Means and variability are extracted from Figure 1.
bias_risk_comments: It is unclear whether the fences exclude all mammals present in the area or not, thus there is the potential for some unaccounted grazing in the exclosure plots by small mammals.

author_list: Raillard, MC; Svoboda, J
title: Exact growth and increased nitrogen compensation by the Arctic sedge Carex aquatilis var. stans after simulated grazing
soil_texture_comments:
Authors say 'The experimental
plots were established in a meadow dominated by Carex
aquatilis. These stands have developed on coarse gravel beds.
Peat layers are 15 to 25 cm deep'
habitat_type_comments:
Described as 'The ground
thaws to a maximum depth of about 25 cm and is covered by
0.5 to 3 cm of water during the growing season
study_design_comments:
Experimental: Two large exclosures (1.5 m X 12 m X 40 cm) were established
in a stand of Carex aquatilis var. stans. Plots of 50 cm
X 100 cm inside the exclosures were randomly assigned to one
of six clipping treatments. Here I report the contrast between unclipped plots and plots clipped only once every year (late season)

Note: response variables were measured each year by clipping the vegetation in August. Since control plots were clipped only at the end of the experiment (1988), this is the only comparison that can be reported here (i.e. after three years). The comparison is reported as an average of the clipped plots (separately for the different treatment combinations, i.e. clipping frequencies) against unclipped (control) plots.
herbivore_data_comments:
Described as 'The valley supported a muskox population of about 50 animals
during the study period (Raillard, 1992).'
measured_response_variable: Cumulative production in biomass (green and dead) above 1.5 cm
measured_response_comments: Average cumulative production over three years in plots clipped once per year (higher diversity) vs unclipped plots (lower diversity)
bias_risk_comments:
C1: Authors controlled both for connections between tillers inside and outside experimental plots by trenching the edge of each plot and for edge effects by discarding a 15 cm perimeter around each plot.
C2: medium risk because plots were established inside two large exclosures, which should be considered the experimental units. Thus, though the number of plots per treatment combination was 4, two sub-replicates were established within the same exclosure. In other words, the study might suffer of weak pseudo-replication.
C7: for the same reason given for C2, and because it does not appear that pseudo-replication was taken into consideration, I here gave medium risk.

author_list: JONSDOTTIR, IS
title: EFFECTS OF GRAZING ON TILLER SIZE AND POPULATION DYNAMICS IN A CLONAL SEDGE (CAREX BIGELOWII)
study_design_comments: only one fence at each site
diversity_contrast_comments: exclosure was open to autumn grazing, but one area remained ungrazed
more_data: there is also information on population flux (birth rate, death rate, rate of increase…) for C bigelowii (Table 3) but no errors are provided for the measurements. As well other population dynamics measures, but difficult to extract information, and information on mean dry weight of different fractions (rhizome vs shoot) for individuals in different age classes…
bias_risk_comments: CRITERION 1. site selection seems a bit tricky because the fenced area was open to autumn grazing except some particular areas that remained ungrazed where the sampling was conducted, but other confounding variables could play a role (e.g. topography, soil moisture), and are not taken into account. CRITERION 2. unclear how sites were selected (but plots within the sites were placed randomly). CRITERION 5. unclear whether the researchers were aware of the treatments when measuring in the field. CRITERION 7. unclear whether analyst was aware of levels of herbivore diversity received by the study units.

quantitative_synthesis: not possible to estimate effect size

title: Interactions between gray-sided voles (Clethrionomys rufucanus) and bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus), their main winter food plant
locality: The shores of Lake Iešjávri (islands and mainlaind), Finnmarksvidda
habitat_type_comments: three tundra habitats pooled: bog hummocks, lichen heaths, windswept ridge tops with scattered dwarf-shrubs
herbivore_data_comments: Vole densities were recorded twice a year from 2000 to 2003 using vole traps. Other herbivores are listed by authors.
comment: Here, low diversity refers to vole-free islands and high diversity to mainland. Data for predator-free islands is also presented, but the herbivore diversity is the same as in mainland. ICB: hares and grouse fo not occur in small islands (vole-free islands) --> low diversity is thus zero
bias_risk_comments: CRITERION 2 & 3 voles were quantified, but about hares and grouses authors said that they occur the in mainland and large islands. However, some of the vole-free islands (low diversity) were defined as small.

author_list: Olofsson, J.; Shams, H.
title: Determinants of plant species richness in an alpine meadow
habitat_type_comments: Vegetation dominated by graminoids and forbs and an almost continuous layer of moss covers the ground.
diversity_contrast_comments: The mowing treatment involved cutting the vegetation to 2 cm above either the ground or the moss layer in early summer (between 3 July and 11 July, 2002–05). Reindeer were excluded from the blocks but smaller herbivores had free access to the vegetation.
herbivore_data_comments:
Voles and lemmings are
the most important wild herbivores, and they have pronounced effects on the vegetation, especially in winter
(Olofsson et al. 2004)
comment: This study includes other manipulations including fertilization and disturbance. only the mowing experiment simulating herbivory is reported here.
measured_response_comments: Only reporting last year value here (2005)
bias_risk_comments: "Reindeer were excluded from the blocks, but smaller herbivores had free access to the vegetation." Not clear if the small herbivores could only access the mowed and/or the unmowed plots. Also, the mowing treatment does not mimic the selectivity of reindeer grazing

measured_response_comments: species richness in concave growing conditions
bias_risk_comments: CRITERION 2: grazed/ungrazed tretment defined as differnt valleys with different grazing pressure - possible confounding effect as the valleys could have different growing conditions/environmental drivers. CRITERION 3or4: historical records of grazing pressure in ungrazed valleys not known, the valleys might have been influenced by grazing before although they are not currently grazed. Also number of sheep based on records from farmers, not quantified by author.

[The effects of reindeer husbandry and nature conservation in the Malla national park, section 2.5 Välimäki: The effects of reideer grazing on Lepidoptera community structure in two northern Fennoscandian fjells.]
locality: Kilpisjärvi, two fjells: Malla (no reindeer grazing) and Saana (grazed)
study_design_comments: Authors state that climate conditions does not differ between two sites, thus not affecting the results.
herbivore_data_comments: The authors of this section report only if reindeer is present or not. Birds and small mammals are mentioned in other sections of the report.
comment: Sampling frequency: Lepidoptera were collected during four days in each sampling plot, but authors provide one value per plot
outcome_comments: variabilities and U values were not available
bias_risk_comments: CRITERION 1 Authors measured environmental variables affecting Lepidoptera communities, but they were not included as covariates in statistical testings; CRITERION 3 herbivore diversity not quantified
